99.title: Facing the House
99.hook: wherever you are, you face the Ka'ba in Mecca
99.howItsDone: Muslims face the Ka'ba in Mecca for every prayer; mosques mark the direction with a niche called the mihrab, and many people use a compass or a phone app when they pray away from home.

segments.voice: Yesterday: taharah, cleanness of body, clothes and place. Your line was a clean corner. Did you leave one small spot clearer than you found it? Day ninety-nine.

A hotel room in Istanbul. On the ceiling above the bed, or on a little sticker by the desk, there's an arrow. It isn't pointing to the exit. In Chicago, someone opens a prayer app, and a compass needle swings and settles. In a mosque, there's a niche in one wall, the mihrab, and every line of people stands facing it. Starting points all over the earth, and all of them turning toward one small building in one valley. Today: the direction everyone faces.
screen: `AN ARROW IN A HOTEL ROOM.` → `A NICHE IN THE WALL.` → `ALL FACING ONE BUILDING.`

segments.voice: The word is qiblah, the direction a person faces in prayer. It comes from a root that means to face, to be in front of. The qiblah is the Ka'ba, the cube-shaped House in Mecca that the Qur'an says Ibrahim and Isma'il raised. But it wasn't always. A hadith in Bukhari says that after the move to Medina, for sixteen or seventeen months, the Muslims prayed facing Jerusalem. Then, the Qur'an says in Surah al-Baqarah, the Prophet ﷺ kept turning his face toward the sky, and the verse came: turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque, and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it. The hadith collections tell what happened next. A man who had prayed with the Prophet passed a mosque where people were in the middle of their prayer, still facing Jerusalem, and told them. And they turned around, mid-prayer, to face Mecca. There's a mosque in Medina still called the Mosque of the Two Qiblahs. Here's the idea underneath. Earlier in the same surah, the Qur'an says that the East and the West belong to Allah, and wherever you turn, there is His face. So Muslims don't say God lives in the Ka'ba. The direction isn't about where God is. It's about where the people are pointed: one direction, so a worshipper in Jakarta and one in Lagos are part of the same line. And here's an honest wrinkle. From North America, people work out the direction two ways. Along the shortest path over the curve of the globe, Mecca is to the northeast. Along a straight line drawn on a flat map, it's to the southeast. Communities have followed each, and both are trying to face the same House.
screen: `QIBLAH — THE DIRECTION YOU FACE.` · `FIRST JERUSALEM, THEN MECCA.` · `THEY TURNED IN THE MIDDLE OF PRAYER.` · `WHEREVER YOU TURN, HIS FACE.` · then, large: `ONE DIRECTION, ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the qiblah from where you are. If you have a compass or a phone app, use it. If not, just work it out roughly: Mecca is in western Arabia, so from Europe it's roughly southeast, from India roughly west, and from North America northeast or southeast, depending on the method your community follows. Turn your body that way. Stand or sit still for a moment. Picture the lines of people all over the earth, all facing the same point you are. If you pray, this is where you'd face. The bell holds the time.
Qiblah. The direction of prayer, toward the Ka'ba in Mecca, turned from Jerusalem in the Prophet's time. Today's word.
Your line: all turned one way. Once today, when you notice which way you're facing, remember the people, somewhere, facing the same point. Day ninety-nine.

100.title: The five times
100.hook: dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset, night, and how the sun sets the clock
100.howItsDone: Muslims pray five obligatory prayers a day, fajr, dhuhr, asr, maghrib and isha, at times set by the sun's position, and, because the times shift daily, they often check a printed timetable or an app.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the qiblah, the direction of prayer, toward the Ka'ba. Your line was all turned one way. Did you notice which way you were facing, even once? Day one hundred.

Day one hundred. Here's a day with five doors in it. The first opens while it's still dark, when the sky just starts to gray. The second, just after the sun passes its highest point. The third, in the long afternoon, when shadows stretch. The fourth, right after the sun disappears. The fifth, when the last red light has gone from the sky. You don't need a clock to find them. You need a window. Today: the five times, and how the sun keeps them.
screen: `DAY ONE HUNDRED.` → `A DAY WITH FIVE DOORS.` → `YOU NEED A WINDOW, NOT A CLOCK.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an says, in Surah an-Nisa, that prayer is enjoined on the believers at fixed times. The five are named from the day itself. Fajr, dawn: from first light until sunrise. Dhuhr, midday: just after the sun passes its peak. Asr, afternoon: when a thing's shadow has grown to its own length, or in the Hanafi school, twice its length. Maghrib, sunset: once the sun is gone. And Isha, night: when the twilight has faded. That's why prayer times change every day, and why a timetable in Oslo looks nothing like one in Nairobi. The sun keeps the clock, not the watch. Where did five come from? A hadith in Bukhari tells it as part of the Night Journey. On the ascent, the Prophet ﷺ was given fifty prayers a day. On his way down, Musa stopped him and said, in effect, your people won't manage that, go back and ask for less. He went back again and again, and it came down to five. And the hadith ends with a line: five in the doing, fifty in the reward. Look where the times fall: waking, the middle of work, the slump of afternoon, the end of the day, the edge of sleep. Five hinges of an ordinary day, and at each one, the prayer. Shia practice allows joining them into three sittings, dawn, midday with afternoon, sunset with night, and Sunni schools allow joining on a journey. It's still five prayers.
screen: `PRAYER AT FIXED TIMES.` · `DAWN, MIDDAY, AFTERNOON, SUNSET, NIGHT.` · `FIFTY BECAME FIVE.` · `AT THE HINGES OF THE DAY.` · then, large: `THE SUN KEEPS THE CLOCK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look up today's five times where you are. A prayer app, a mosque's website, or a search will give them to you. Read them slowly: fajr, dhuhr, asr, maghrib, isha. Notice which one has already passed, and which is next. Then look out a window if you can, and guess where the sun is on that path. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, you can set a small reminder for the next one. The bell holds the time.
The five times. Fajr, dhuhr, asr, maghrib, isha: five prayers, set by the sun, fifty that became five. Today's word.
Your line: the sun keeps the times. When you notice the light change today, at sunset maybe, ask which of the five doors is opening. A hundred days. Day one hundred.

101.title: Allahu akbar
101.hook: hands raised, the prayer opens, the world is set behind you
101.howItsDone: Every Muslim prayer opens with the takbir: raising the hands to the shoulders or ears and saying Allahu akbar, after which the worshipper stays focused on the prayer, not speaking, eating or turning away, until the closing salam.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the five times, dawn to night. Your line was the sun keeps the times. Did you catch the light changing, and wonder which door was opening? Day one hundred one.

You've done the washing. You've found the direction. The time has come in. You're standing on a clean spot, and your phone is still buzzing in your pocket, and half your mind is on an email you didn't finish. Then the person in front raises both hands, palms forward, up by the ears, and says two words. And for the next few minutes, the email doesn't exist. You can't answer the phone. You can't turn to chat. Something has closed behind you like a door. Today: the two words that open the prayer.
screen: `WASHED, FACING, ON TIME.` → `BOTH HANDS RAISED.` → `A DOOR CLOSES BEHIND YOU.`

segments.voice: The words are Allahu akbar, and saying them is called takbir. Most people translate them as God is great. But akbar is a comparative, like bigger or greater. So a closer sense is: God is greater. Greater than what? The sentence doesn't say, and that's the point. Greater than the email. Greater than the worry. Greater than whatever you just walked in carrying. Greater than anything you could put at the end of the sentence. The first takbir of the prayer has its own name: takbirat al-ihram, the takbir of making things forbidden. Ihram is the same word used for a pilgrim's sacred state. Once it's said, ordinary things become off-limits: eating, talking, looking around, anything that isn't the prayer. A hadith in the Sunan collections puts the whole prayer in one sentence: its key is purity, its opening is the takbir, and its closing is the salam. So yesterday's cleanness is the key, and today's words turn it. Then the hands. Most Muslims raise them to the shoulders or to the ears; the schools of law describe it a little differently, and all of them are doing the same thing. Many teachers describe it as throwing the world behind you. And takbir doesn't stay in the prayer. It's in the call to prayer, it's said when a baby is born, on the Eid mornings, on a hilltop. It's the phrase that marks every change of position in the prayer, as you'll hear over the next few days. It's the hinge the whole prayer turns on.
screen: `AKBAR — NOT GREAT, GREATER.` · `THE TAKBIR THAT FORBIDS.` · `ITS OPENING IS THE TAKBIR.` · `THE WORLD SET BEHIND YOU.` · then, large: `GREATER THAN ALL OF IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand, if you can. Let your arms hang for a moment. Think of the one thing tugging at you most right now. Name it silently. Then raise both hands, palms forward, to your shoulders or your ears. If you pray, you can say it once, Allahu akbar, quietly. If not, just raise your hands and notice the feeling of setting something behind you. Lower them, and let the next two minutes be empty of that thing. The bell holds the time.
Takbir. Saying Allahu akbar, God is greater: the opening of the prayer, the door that closes behind you. Today's word.
Your line: greater than all of it. When something today feels like the biggest thing in the room, finish the sentence in your head: greater than this. Day one hundred one.

102.title: Standing and reciting
102.hook: you stand and recite al-Fatiha, then a short surah
102.howItsDone: In each unit of prayer, Muslims stand and recite al-Fatiha in Arabic, adding another passage of the Qur'an in the first two units; at dawn, sunset and night the leader recites the first two units aloud.

segments.voice: Yesterday: takbir, Allahu akbar, hands raised, the prayer opened. Your line was greater than all of it. Did you finish that sentence in your head, even once? Day one hundred two.

The hands come down. In some schools, they fold over the body; in others, they rest at the sides. The eyes drop to the spot where the forehead will touch the ground. And then, for the first time in the prayer, the person speaks at length. Not a speech. Not a list of requests. A short chapter you first met back in the first week of this path, the one that asks for directions. Standing still, in front of no one you can see, saying it as if someone is listening. Today: the standing.
screen: `THE HANDS COME DOWN.` → `EYES ON THE PLACE OF PROSTRATION.` → `THEN THE FIRST WORDS.`

segments.voice: The standing is called qiyam, from a root that means to stand up, to rise, to stand firm. In it, every unit of the prayer begins with al-Fatiha, the Opening. A hadith in Bukhari is blunt about it: there's no prayer for the one who doesn't recite the Opening of the Book. So it comes back in every unit of every prayer. It begins, in Pickthall's translation: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." And at its center: "Thee (alone) we worship; Thee (alone) we ask for help." Now the surprise. A hadith qudsi in Sahih Muslim, where the Prophet ﷺ relays words from God, says the prayer is divided between God and the one praying. When the person says, praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds, God says: My servant has praised Me. When they say, the Beneficent, the Merciful: My servant has extolled Me. And at the middle line: this is between Me and My servant, and My servant will have what he asks. So the standing isn't a recital into empty air. In the tradition's own telling, it's a conversation, answered line by line. After the Fatiha, in the first two units, the person adds some other part of the Qur'an, often a short surah from the end of the book, like al-Ikhlas, four lines long. At dawn, sunset and night, the first two units are recited aloud by the one leading. At midday and afternoon, silently. Either way, the person stands, and speaks, and, in the hadith's telling, is answered.
screen: `QIYAM — TO STAND, TO STAND FIRM.` · `NO PRAYER WITHOUT THE OPENING.` · `MY SERVANT HAS PRAISED ME.` · `THEN A SHORT SURAH.` · then, large: `STAND, SPEAK, BE ANSWERED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand still. Feet a little apart, hands folded or at your sides, eyes resting on a spot on the floor in front of you. If you know the Fatiha, recite it slowly, and leave a small pause after each line, as if waiting for the answer. If you don't know it, say just the first line from Pickthall's translation, praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds, and stand in the quiet after it. The bell holds the time.
Qiyam. The standing in prayer, where the Fatiha is recited, then a short surah. Today's word.
Your line: stand and speak. Once today, before you say something that matters, stand up straight first, and say it like someone's listening. Day one hundred two.

103.title: The bow
103.hook: back straight, hands on knees, glory to my Lord the Great
103.howItsDone: After reciting, Muslims say Allahu akbar and bow with hands on their knees and back level, usually saying subhana rabbiya al-'azim three times, and remaining still in the bow before rising.

segments.voice: Yesterday: qiyam, the standing, the Fatiha answered line by line. Your line was stand and speak. Did you stand up straight before saying something that mattered? Day one hundred three.

A man walks into the mosque in Medina and prays, quickly. Then he comes over to the Prophet ﷺ and greets him with salaam. The Prophet returns the greeting, and then says something the man didn't expect: go back and pray, because you haven't prayed. In a bow, the body can look finished before it has arrived. A dip of the head and shoulders, and it's over. Today: the bow, and what that man was missing.
screen: `A MAN PRAYS QUICKLY.` → `HE GREETS THE PROPHET.` → `GO BACK AND PRAY.`

segments.voice: The bow is called ruku', from a root that means to bend, to bow down. After the recitation, the person says Allahu akbar and bends forward from the hips, hands on the knees, back level, head in line with the back. And there, usually three times, they say: subhana rabbiya al-'azim. Glory to my Lord, the Magnificent, the Great. A report in the Sunan says that when a verse came telling the Prophet to glorify the name of his Lord, the Tremendous, he said: put it in your bowing. Now back to the man in the mosque. The hadith is in Bukhari. He went back and prayed, and came again, and was told again: go back and pray, you haven't prayed. Three times. Finally he said: by the One who sent you with the truth, I don't know any better, so teach me. And the Prophet did. Among the things he said: bow until you are at rest in your bowing. That's the missing piece. There's a word for it, tuma'nina, stillness, settling. The body has to arrive in the bow before it leaves. Why does it matter? A bow that's only a dip is a gesture. A bow that settles says, with the whole spine, that the one bowing isn't in a hurry to stand back up. And in the tradition, a Muslim bows like this to God alone. Not to a king, not to a teacher, not to a parent. That's the sense in which the bow is honest: it means what it shows, and it's aimed where the tradition says it belongs.
screen: `RUKU' — TO BEND, TO BOW DOWN.` · `GLORY TO MY LORD, THE GREAT.` · `YOU HAVEN'T PRAYED. GO BACK.` · `BOW UNTIL YOU ARE AT REST.` · then, large: `A BOW THAT SETTLES IS HONEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bow once, and settle. Stand, then bend forward from the hips, hands resting on your knees, back as level as it comfortably goes. If your back won't allow it, bow your head and shoulders instead. Stay there. Let your breath slow. If you pray, you can say it three times, subhana rabbiya al-'azim, glory to my Lord the Great. If not, count three slow breaths. Then stand, and sit. The bell holds the time.
Ruku'. The bow in prayer: back level, hands on knees, and still enough to be at rest. Today's word.
Your line: bowing is honest. Today, when you catch yourself rushing something that deserves care, slow down until you're at rest in it. Day one hundred three.

104.title: Rising from the bow
104.hook: you rise saying Allah hears whoever praises Him
104.howItsDone: Rising from the bow, the prayer leader says sami'a Allahu liman hamidah, and the congregation, standing straight and still, responds rabbana wa laka al-hamd before going down to prostrate.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ruku', the bow, back level, still enough to be at rest. Your line was bowing is honest. Did you slow down in something today until you were at rest in it? Day one hundred four.

A message marked read, and no reply. A joke at dinner that lands on nobody. A voicemail that may never be played. A lot of what gets said goes out with no sign of where it lands. In the prayer, the bow is over now. The body comes back up. And on the way up, before the person is even straight, the one leading says a sentence about exactly that. Not a request. A statement. Today: rising from the bow.
screen: `A MESSAGE MARKED READ.` → `NO REPLY.` → `A SENTENCE ON THE WAY UP.`

segments.voice: Rising from the bow, the one leading the prayer says: sami'a Allahu liman hamidah. Allah hears whoever praises Him. Sami'a means He heard, He hears, with the sense of listening and answering. And then, standing straight, the people answer: rabbana wa laka al-hamd. Our Lord, and to You be the praise. Notice the shape. One voice says God hears. Everyone replies with praise, as if to say, then hear this. The scholars call this standing position i'tidal, straightening, and just like the bow, it isn't a pass-through. The same hadith from yesterday, the man who prayed too fast, includes it: rise until you are standing straight. Now the story that makes this moment famous. It's in Bukhari, from a companion named Rifa'a ibn Rafi'. One day, praying behind the Prophet ﷺ, a man rose from the bow and, after our Lord and to You be the praise, added a few words of his own: praise, abundant, good and blessed. When the prayer ended, the Prophet asked who had said it. The man said, I did. And the Prophet said he had seen thirty-some angels racing each other to be the first to write it down. One person, one sentence of praise in the middle of a line of worshippers, and in the hadith, angels hurry to be first to record it. In the tradition's reading, that is what sami'a Allahu liman hamidah promises: praise doesn't vanish into the room. It is heard.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bow, then rise slowly. Stand, bend forward with your hands on your knees, and hold for a breath. Then come up, slowly, a little at a time, until you're straight. As you rise, if you pray, whisper it: sami'a Allahu liman hamidah. Then, standing: rabbana wa laka al-hamd. If you don't, just notice the moment of arriving upright, and stay there, straight and still, for three breaths before you sit. The bell holds the time.
Rising from the bow. Allah hears whoever praises Him, and the answer: our Lord, and to You be the praise. Today's word.
Your line: he hears. Today, when something you say seems to land on nobody, remember the man whose one sentence the angels raced to write. Day one hundred four.

105.title: The prostration
105.hook: forehead on the ground, glory to my Lord the Most High, the closest a person gets
105.howItsDone: In each unit of prayer, Muslims prostrate twice on seven points (forehead and nose, hands, knees, toes), usually saying subhana rabbiya al-a'la three times, and some add their own supplications there silently.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rising from the bow. Allah hears whoever praises Him. Your line was he hears. Did something you said today seem to land on nobody, and did you remember the angels? Day one hundred five.

A direction to face. Five times set by the sun. Two words that close a door behind you. Standing, and speaking, and being answered. A bow that settles. Rising, and being heard. That's this week, and every day the body has gone a little lower. Now it goes all the way down. Knees, then hands, then the forehead on the floor. The highest part of a person, the part with the face and the mind in it, placed on the same ground you walk on. In a wrestling match, ending up face-down is losing. In the prayer, it's the moment of nearness. Today: the prostration.
screen: `A WEEK, LOWER EVERY DAY.` → `NOW ALL THE WAY DOWN.` → `THE FOREHEAD ON THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: The word is sujud, prostration. The same root gives masjid, the Arabic word behind mosque: the place of prostration. The whole building is named for this one moment. A hadith in Bukhari describes how it's done: on seven bones. The forehead, with the nose. The two hands. The two knees. And the toes of both feet. Seven points of the body touching the earth. And every unit of the prayer has two of them. There, usually three times, the person says: subhana rabbiya al-a'la. Glory to my Lord, the Most High. Notice the pairing. In the bow, you said the Great. Now, at the lowest point your body can reach, you say the Most High. The lower you go, the higher the name. Then the hadith that gives today its line. It's in Sahih Muslim. The Prophet ﷺ said: the closest a servant is to his Lord is while prostrating, so make much supplication there. The closest. Not standing tall. Not at the head of a line. Face on the floor. The hadith points there for a person's own requests, said silently. Surah al-Alaq, the surah that begins with Read, ends on the same idea: prostrate yourself, and draw near. All week the body has gone lower. In the hadith, the lowest point is the nearest.
screen: `SUJUD — THE MASJID IS NAMED FOR IT.` · `SEVEN BONES ON THE EARTH.` · `GLORY TO MY LORD, THE MOST HIGH.` · `THE CLOSEST A SERVANT IS.` · then, large: `PROSTRATE, AND DRAW NEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one prostration, unhurried. If your body allows, kneel, place your hands flat on the floor, and lower your forehead and nose to the ground. If it doesn't, sit and bow your head as low as is comfortable; that counts too. Stay there. Feel the seven points, or however many are touching. If you pray, you can say subhana rabbiya al-a'la, three times, and then ask for one thing, in your own words. Then just rest there. The bell holds the time.
Sujud. Prostration: forehead on the ground, glory to my Lord the Most High, the closest a person gets. Today's word.

Your line: closest when lowest. When you feel small today, brought low by something, try hearing it the tradition's way: this might be the closest place. A week of the prayer, done. Day one hundred five.

original.note: Arabic: prostration. The same root gives masjid (مَسْجِد), the place of prostration.

trapdoor: what you thought: Muslims bow down with their heads on the floor.
what it means: sujud is the lowest posture and, in the hadith, the closest a person gets to God.
what a scholar hears: sajada gives masjid; the seven bones (Bukhari 812); Muslim 482 on nearness; and 96:19 ending on prostrate and draw near.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 482 (the closest a servant is to his Lord is while prostrating)

Qur'an 96:19 (prostrate yourself, and draw near)
